result:
The proposed answer, t = q^h − 1, is not justified, and I believe it is wrong.

The solution cites no actual theorem. It says the value is "the largest power of q minus 1" and gives only a vague claim about "scaling and structural constraints". That is a guess, not a derivation.

I tried to test the answer with a counting check for h = 1, k = 4, which is a set of points in PG(3,q) with at most t on any plane. Counting planes through a fixed point gives (q+1)(n−1) ≤ (q²+q+1)(t−1). Both t = q−1 and t = q satisfy this, so the check does not decide between them.

Structural reasoning points away from q^h − 1 for h > 1. Maximal-arc-type extremal configurations normally force t to be a multiple of q^{h−1}, because the hyperplane intersection numbers are constrained modulo q^{h−1}. The value q^h − 1 is not a multiple of q^{h−1} when h > 1. A value such as q^h − q^{h−1} would fit that constraint, and it agrees with q^h − 1 only at h = 1. I could not recall the actual theorem, so I cannot confirm that value either.

VERDICT: REJECT
